name: French

ancestors.notes: Frankish superstrate: /h/ restoration, initial stress, massive vocabulary (guerre, jardin, blanc). Strongest in Romance.
Gaulish substrate (already in la-x-gallia, additional direct traces)

notes: Standard Metropolitan French (Parisian). Nasal grapheme sequences (⟨an⟩, ⟨am⟩, ⟨en⟩, ⟨em⟩, ⟨in⟩, ⟨im⟩, ⟨on⟩, ⟨om⟩, ⟨un⟩, ⟨um⟩) denasalise before a following vowel within the word (positional_graphemes before_vowel branch, e.g. amateur [amatœʁ], inutile [inytil], bonasse [bɔnas]); the ⟨n⟩/⟨m⟩-doubling trigger for denasalisation (immense, ennemi) is not separately modelled because the doubled consonant is tokenised as its own bb/dd/ff/gg/ll/mm/nn/pp/rr/tt digraph rather than surfacing as BEFORE_VOWEL/BEFORE_CONSONANT context on the nasal grapheme — a known engine-limit gap. Word-final unstressed ⟨e⟩ (e caduc) defaults to silent (positional_graphemes word_final), matching modern colloquial elision of the mute e; monosyllabic function words whose sole vowel is that final ⟨e⟩ (le, de, que, ce, ne, se, je, me, te) are handled via the word_exceptions whole-word override, since the positional-grapheme priority order always resolves WORD_FINAL before NUCLEUS_STRESSED and cannot express 'sole vowel nucleus of a monosyllable' as a rule — the schwa is grammatically obligatory there to preserve the syllable. FINAL CONSONANTS: t, d, p, s, x, r typically silent word-finally in modern French, resurfacing in liaison. LIAISON: s/x→[z], d/t→[t], n→[n] before vowel-initial words (sandhi_rules, obligatory after determiners/pronouns, optional after adjectives/prepositions per Tranel 1995). Aspirate-h words (les héros, le hibou) block both liaison and elision (Tranel 1995); this cannot currently be distinguished from mute-h words at the grapheme/sandhi level since ⟨h⟩ maps to the empty string in both cases — a lexical h-aspiré wordlist would be required, out of scope for this pass. Elision (le/la/je/de/que + vowel → l'/j'/d'/qu') is already resolved in standard orthography (words are written with the apostrophe), so it needs no additional G2P rule. SOFTENING: c→[s] before e/i/y; g→[ʒ] before e/i/y. INTERVOCALIC s: [z] between vowels within a word. Doubled consonants (bb, dd, ff, gg, ll, mm, nn, pp, rr, tt) degeminate to a single consonant, the modern-French default (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987). Modern Parisian speech increasingly merges /œ̃/ into /ɛ̃/ (brun/brin, un/hein); both realizations are kept as allophones of œ̃ rather than collapsing the phonemic contrast, since conservative Standard French sources (Fougeron & Smith 1993) still treat them as distinct. GLIDE FORMATION: word-internal ⟨i⟩ before another vowel letter glides to [j] (pied [pje], lion [ljɔ̃], fiacre [fjakʁ]) — positional_graphemes before_vowel branch, Tranel (1987) §5-6 on high-vowel gliding; the plain vowel-letter ⟨i⟩ (unlike the ⟨y⟩/⟨ien⟩/⟨oui⟩ digraphs already carrying [j]) previously always surfaced as the full vowel. This is blocked (BEFORE_FINAL_VOWEL, an engine-level position, see orthography2ipa/types.py) when the following vowel is itself the word's last audible slot — word-final unmarked ⟨ie⟩ stays [i], not [j+deleted-e]: vie [vi], envie [ɑ̃vi], folie [fɔli], Algérie [alʒeʁi], and the plural vies [vi] (⟨s⟩ is a transparent, independently-silenced suffix grapheme, Tranel 1987 §3) — without this exclusion the glide rule wrongly produces a vowel-less [vj] for the entire closed class of French nouns ending in unstressed ⟨-ie⟩/⟨-ies⟩. ILL EXCEPTION CLASS: ⟨ill⟩ is [ij] by default (fille, famille, bastille) except in a closed irregular set where it stays [il] — ville, mille, tranquille (and tranquillement) and the place name Lille — handled via word_exceptions per Tranel (1987) §4.3's irregular-ill list, since the digraph mapping cannot express a lexical exception to its own default. Sources: Fouché (1959), Tranel (1987), Ladefoged & Maddieson (1996), Fougeron & Smith (1993), Tranel (1995). word_exceptions also carry Tranel 1987 §7's closed list of common words whose final ⟨s⟩ is exceptionally pronounced (fils [fis], os, ours, mars, maïs, tennis, sens...); regular final ⟨s⟩ stays silent, and ambiguous homographs (tous, plus) are deliberately excluded. MUTE ⟨-er⟩/⟨-ez⟩ ENDINGS: deliberately NOT modelled as grapheme keys. Word-final ⟨-er⟩/[e] (parler) vs /ɛʁ/ (mer, hiver, super, loanwords) and ⟨-ez⟩/[e] (mangez, nez) are a MORPHOLOGICAL split — the mute reading belongs to the infinitive/2pl/agent-noun endings, not to the letter sequence — and morpheme chunks are forbidden grapheme keys (an ⟨er⟩ digraph makes ⟨s⟩ in pers-/vers- look intervocalic → *[pɛʁzɔn], and out-munches ⟨rr⟩ degemination → *[tɛʁʁ]); needs a morpheme-aware engine context (same follow-up as English suffix palatalization). The general word-final ⟨r⟩ silencing above covers the mute class at the letter level; the words whose final ⟨r⟩ IS pronounced (the mer/fer/hiver monosyllable-and-friends set plus English -er loanwords keeping /œʁ/~/ɛʁ/) are lexical exceptions carried in word_exceptions. FINAL ⟨r⟩ IS PRONOUNCED: the earlier word_final [""] made silence the DEFAULT for every final ⟨r⟩, which is the inverse of the fact — French word-final ⟨r⟩ is [ʁ] (mer, bonjour, sur, par, hiver, amour, chanteur); it is mute only in the ⟨-er⟩ sequence (infinitives parler, -er/-ier nouns and adjectives boulanger, premier), and that case is already owned by the grammatical_endings ⟨er⟩→[e] rewrite, which runs after the beam and also absorbs the transparent plural ⟨-ers⟩ (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 §3). word_final is therefore ["ʁ", ""] — pronounced first, silence kept as the second beam branch for the monosyllabic-lexical residue. VERBAL ⟨-ent⟩ IS NOT DECLARED, ON PURPOSE: the 3rd-person-plural inflection ⟨-ent⟩ is silent (ils parlent [paʁl], munissent [mynis]), and a grammatical_endings ⟨ent⟩→[] entry does win 3844 wikipron/fr types against 254 losses. It is NOT shipped, because the 254 are the nominal/adjectival ⟨-ent⟩ class — vent, dent, cent, argent, accent, talent, absent, serpent, Occident, Vincent — which is far commoner in running text than the inflected verb forms it wins, and this library feeds TTS. The class also fails grammatical_endings' own precondition (see types.py): the counter-set must be CLOSED and live in word_exceptions, and French ⟨-ent⟩ nouns/adjectives plus proper nouns (Laurent, Florent, Clément) are open. Verb-vs-noun is not decidable from spelling; it needs part-of-speech, which this layer does not have. Left to a morphology-aware pass. LOI DE POSITION for ⟨eu⟩: [ø] in an open syllable (heureux, peu, jeu), [œ] in a closed one (fleur, chanteur, jeune) — Fougeron & Smith (1993), loi de position; Tranel (1987) ch. 4. Expressed with the OPEN_SYLLABLE/CLOSED_SYLLABLE positions. The same law is NOT declared for ⟨o⟩ and ⟨e⟩: aperture is decided on the ORTHOGRAPHIC syllable, and French's silent final consonants make that proxy wrong exactly where those two vowels need it (⟨eux⟩ and ⟨o⟩ + silent coda look closed and open respectively when they are not); measured on wikipron/fr the ⟨o⟩ rule cost 4.4 PER points, so it is left out rather than shipped half-right.

sources.notes: Documents the ɛ̃/œ̃ merger in Parisian speech (speakers use only /ɛ̃/, especially in northern France) and the loi de position (close-mid e/ø/o in open syllables, open-mid ɛ/œ/ɔ in closed syllables).

sources.author: Tranel, B.
sources.title: French liaison and elision revisited: A unified account within Optimality Theory
sources.notes: Formalises liaison (silent word-final consonant surfaces before a vowel-initial word, e.g. les amis [lezami]) and elision (word-final vowel deleted before a vowel-initial word, e.g. l'ami) as ONSET-driven; establishes that h-aspiré words (hibou) block both liaison and elision despite being phonetically vowel-initial (les hiboux *[lezibu], le hibou *[libu]).

⟨e⟩ in a closed syllable is [ɛ], not schwa (Tranel 1987 §4: loi de position — Abel [abɛl], Albert [albɛʁ], mer, sel); e-caduc only occurs in open syllables. Two conditions cover closure: before a consonant cluster, and before a word-final consonant.

⟨e⟩ in a closed syllable is [ɛ], not schwa (Tranel 1987 §4: loi de position — Abel [abɛl], Albert [albɛʁ], mer, sel); e-caduc only occurs in open syllables. Two conditions cover closure: before a consonant cluster, and before a word-final consonant.

Loi de position for /ɔ/ (Tranel 1987 §3): mid back vowel is close [o] in a word-final open syllable (mot [mo], numéro) and before /z/ (rose [ʁoz], chose); open [ɔ] in other closed syllables (bord, botte).

Loi de position for /ɔ/ (Tranel 1987 §3): mid back vowel is close [o] in a word-final open syllable (mot [mo], numéro) and before /z/ (rose [ʁoz], chose); open [ɔ] in other closed syllables (bord, botte).
